"Tighten Up" is a song by R&B vocal group Archie Bell & the Drells. Released in 1968, it reached No. 1 on both the Billboard R&B and pop charts in the spring of 1968. It is ranked No. 265 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time and is one of the earliest funk hits in music history.

sections.heading: History
sections.wikitext:
"Tighten Up" was written by [[Archie Bell (singer)|Archie Bell]] and Billy Butler.<ref name="The Book of Golden Discs">{{cite book
| first= Joseph
| last= Murrells
| year= 1978
| title= The Book of Golden Discs
| edition= 2nd
| publisher= Barrie and Jenkins Ltd
| location= London
| page= [https://archive.org/details/bookofgoldendisc00murr/page/236 236]
| isbn= 0-214-20512-6
| url-access= registration
| url= https://archive.org/details/bookofgoldendisc00murr/page/236
}}</ref> It was one of the first songs that [[Archie Bell & the Drells]] recorded, in a session in August 1967 at the Jones Town Studio in Houston, Texas, along with a number of songs including "She's My Woman". The instrumental backing for "Tighten Up" was provided by the T.S.U. Toronadoes, the group which had developed it<ref>
{{cite web
  | last = Boone
  | first = Mike
  | publisher = Soul-Patrol Newsletter
  | title = Historical ANalysis - Archie Bell & The Drells
  | url = http://www.soul-patrol.com/philly/archie.html
  | accessdate = 30 April 2006 }}
</ref> in their own live shows before they brought it to Archie Bell & the Drells at the suggestion of Skipper Lee Frazier, a Houston disc jockey who worked with both groups. At the recording session, the Drells worked late into the night with the Toronadoes as Archie Bell perfected the vocals.<ref name="1967disc">
{{cite web
  | publisher = Jazz Discography Project.
  | title = Atlantic Records Discography: 1967
  | url=https://www.jazzdisco.org/atlantic-records/discography-1967/#671000
  | accessdate = 30 October 2011 }}
</ref><ref>
{{Citation
  | last1 = Gray
  | first1 = Chris
  | last2 = Koshkin
  | first2 = Brett
  | title = The TSU Toronadoes: The twisted history of "Tighten Up"
  | newspaper = Houston Press
  | date = 12 December 2007
  | url=https://www.houstonpress.com/2007-12-13/news/the-tsu-toronadoes/
  | accessdate = 30 October 2011 }}
</ref>

Soon afterwards, Bell was drafted into the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] and began serving in [[Vietnam War|Vietnam]]. Meanwhile, the song became a hit in Houston, and was picked up by [[Atlantic Records]] for distribution in April 1968. By the summer it topped both the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|R&B]] and [[Billboard Hot 100|pop]] [[record chart|charts]]. It also sold a million copies by May 1968, gaining an [[Recording Industry Association of America|RIAA]] [[music recording sales certification|gold disc]].<ref name="The Book of Golden Discs"/>

In the beginning of the song, Bell introduces himself and the Drells as being from [[Houston]], [[Texas]]. According to the ''Billboard Book of Number One Hits'' by [[Fred Bronson]], Bell had heard a comment after the [[Kennedy assassination]] in Dallas that "nothing good ever came out of Texas." Bell wanted his listeners to know "we were from Texas and we were good."{{cn|date=November 2022}}

Although their leader was unavailable, the success of the [[single (music)|single]] prompted the band to rush out their first album, which included the songs they had recorded in late 1967 and early 1968 with the Toronadoes.<ref name="1967disc"/><ref>
{{cite web
  | publisher = Jazz Discography Project.
  | title = Atlantic Records Discography: 1968
  | url=https://www.jazzdisco.org/atlantic-records/discography-1968/
  | accessdate = 30 October 2011 }}
</ref>

In 1969, the group recorded their first full album with [[Gamble and Huff]], ''I Can't Stop Dancing'', which reached No. 28 on the [[R&B chart]].

At the [[Athletics at the 1968 Summer Olympics – Women's 100 metres|1968 Olympics]], American Olympian [[Wyomia Tyus]] was doing a dance waiting at the start line of the 100 meter race in which she became the first person in the event to regain the Olympic championship.  When interviewed later by Olympic documentarian [[Bud Greenspan]] about what she was doing, she credited dancing to this song, a current hit at the time that was being sung and played on bongos by American fans near the start line.<ref>{{cite web|author= |url=https://speedendurance.com/2010/06/16/wyomia-tyus-the-famous-pre-race-dance-to-out-psych-everyone/ |title=Wyomia Tyus: The Famous Pre-Race Dance to Out-Psych Everyone |website=Speedendurance.com |date=2010-06-16 |accessdate=2016-10-02}}</ref>

In 1980, Japanese [[Electronic music|electronic music]] band [[Yellow Magic Orchestra]] released a [[synth-funk]] cover titled "Tighten Up (Japanese Gentlemen Stand Up Please)" which was included in the album ''[[X∞Multiplies]]''. It was also released as a single and reached number 43 on the [[Oricon Singles Chart]] and sold 38,000 copies in Japan.<ref name="oricon_single_archive">{{cite web |title=Yellow Magic Orchestra (Singles) |url=http://www7a.biglobe.ne.jp/~yamag/single/ymo.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071016164243/www7a.biglobe.ne.jp/~yamag/single/ymo.html |archive-date=2007-10-16 |access-date=June 1, 2011 |website=Yamachan Land |publisher=[[Oricon]] |language=ja}}</ref>
sections.text:
"Tighten Up" was written by Archie Bell and Billy Butler. It was one of the first songs that Archie Bell & the Drells recorded, in a session in August 1967 at the Jones Town Studio in Houston, Texas, along with a number of songs including "She's My Woman". The instrumental backing for "Tighten Up" was provided by the T.S.U. Toronadoes, the group which had developed it in their own live shows before they brought it to Archie Bell & the Drells at the suggestion of Skipper Lee Frazier, a Houston disc jockey who worked with both groups. At the recording session, the Drells worked late into the night with the Toronadoes as Archie Bell perfected the vocals.

Soon afterwards, Bell was drafted into the U.S. Army and began serving in Vietnam. Meanwhile, the song became a hit in Houston, and was picked up by Atlantic Records for distribution in April 1968. By the summer it topped both the Billboard R&B and pop charts. It also sold a million copies by May 1968, gaining an RIAA gold disc.

In the beginning of the song, Bell introduces himself and the Drells as being from Houston, Texas. According to the Billboard Book of Number One Hits by Fred Bronson, Bell had heard a comment after the Kennedy assassination in Dallas that "nothing good ever came out of Texas." Bell wanted his listeners to know "we were from Texas and we were good."{{cn|date=November 2022}}

Although their leader was unavailable, the success of the single prompted the band to rush out their first album, which included the songs they had recorded in late 1967 and early 1968 with the Toronadoes.

In 1969, the group recorded their first full album with Gamble and Huff, I Can't Stop Dancing, which reached No. 28 on the R&B chart.

At the 1968 Olympics, American Olympian Wyomia Tyus was doing a dance waiting at the start line of the 100 meter race in which she became the first person in the event to regain the Olympic championship.  When interviewed later by Olympic documentarian Bud Greenspan about what she was doing, she credited dancing to this song, a current hit at the time that was being sung and played on bongos by American fans near the start line.

In 1980, Japanese electronic music band Yellow Magic Orchestra released a synth-funk cover titled "Tighten Up (Japanese Gentlemen Stand Up Please)" which was included in the album X∞Multiplies. It was also released as a single and reached number 43 on the Oricon Singles Chart and sold 38,000 copies in Japan.
